what: A second correct form that the key marks wrong
reader: For every typed gap and every bank, try each other tense in the sentence. c-3118: She ___ in Madrid very long, but she knew the city well. (not / live): 'didn't live' is correct too. Fix with a situation (When I first met her … already), not by widening the key when the task is about one form.

what: Correct English marked wrong by a word bank
reader: Coffee ___ in Brazil (grows is correct), Two windows ___ in the storm (broke is correct), Mr Ozols asked whether the invoices ___ ___ sent (have been is correct). Read the sentence with every chip and every pair of chips.

what: An open gap that several words fit
reader: ___ you help me? takes can / could / will / would; There was ___ much traffic takes too / so. Use a choice with one fitting option, or accept every word.

what: The question and the answer are about different people
reader: ppc-B11-5a: 'Your friend is out of breath … Which sentence explains why?' with the answer 'I've been running.' Check who speaks in the answer.

what: Two matching pairs whose meanings can be swapped
reader: has been repaired = the work is finished / was repaired = it happened in the past; a plan / an arrangement. Swap any two right-hand sides: if both versions make sense, rewrite.

what: Two sentences joined with a comma in the task text
reader: fu-B11-5a: 'I will meet Anna at 6, we agreed yesterday.' The task text itself must be correct English.

what: A wrong option that nobody would choose, or that is correct English
reader: I meet Anna at 6 yesterday; The agent said I mighted need a visa. And the opposite: will freeze after 'If water gets very cold, it ___'. Each wrong option is a real form that a learner might choose and that is wrong in this sentence.

what: A report that is not a mistake
reader: c-0409: 'I was doing the shopping' was reported as wrong; do the shopping is correct (Murphy). Do not change correct English because of a report: check first.

what: The level label does not fit the sentence
reader: C1.1: We couldn't decide where ___ on holiday. (go). Compare the grammar and the words with docs/LEVEL-LISTS-test-english.md before giving a level.

what: A rewording that loses who is spoken to
reader: 'Report this request. Start with She: Please close the window.' Without 'to me', She asked him / us to close the window is as right as She asked me. When a tag is removed, check that the speaker AND the person spoken to are still known.

what: The moment of speaking is not fixed
reader: fu-B11-5a draft: 'A colleague asks about your evening.' Asked the next morning, I met Anna at 6 is the right answer. Say when (At lunch … your plans for this evening).

what: A reported statement that is still true
reader: 'I don't like coffee.' → Mark said he ___ coffee: doesn't like is correct too while it is still true. Give a situation that ends it (Ten years ago … Now he drinks it every day) or accept it with a note.

what: Generated word orders in a key that are not natural English or change the meaning
reader: If I liked jazz, he asked me. / The next day they said they would finish the report. Read every accepted answer of a typed task aloud; a start (Start with He asked me) must fit every accepted answer.

what: A task that can be solved without the grammar it is about (teacher, 11 November)
reader: Ask of every task: what does the learner have to know to get it right? 'I've been to Italy twice. = I have visited it two times in my life.' is matched by the word two. A choice whose three wrong options are in another time (I've met / I was meeting / I met for a plan this evening) is solved without knowing the future forms: the wrong options must compete (I'm meeting / I'll meet / I meet). A long situation in front of an easy choice is the same fault.

what: An instruction the learner may not understand
reader: 'Report it. Start with He asked me.' Learners may not know report. Show the quote and the start of the answer and let them complete it: 'Do you like jazz?' → He asked me ___.

what: An accepted word order that nobody says
reader: before it gets dark should we leave (generated). Read every accepted alternative aloud.

what: A typed conditional with both parts open and no situation
reader: If I ___ harder, I ___ the test. (study / pass): studied / would pass is as correct as had studied / would have passed. One situation sentence decides (I failed the test last week.).

what: A joining task that is only copying
reader: Join with if: You leave now. You will catch the train. At B1 the learner must change something (Leave now or you'll miss the train → If you don't leave now, …).

what: c-0737: If I ___ harder, I ___ the test. (study / pass): only had studied / would have passed accepted, but studied / would pass is correct too (report of 11 November)

task.q: If I ___ harder, I ___ the test. (study / pass)

what: The same mistake with the result first: I ___ her if I ___ her address. (visit / know) (11 November)

task.q: I ___ her if I ___ her address. (visit / know)

what: A situation sentence that leaves the first conditional possible (second reader, 12 November)
reader: 'Our company has fixed hours. If the company ___ more flexible hours, people ___ happier.' A fact that can still change allows offers / will be. The situation must make the condition unreal (will never change) or past.

what: The instruction names the answer (second reader, 12 November)
reader: 'Which sentence reports Sam's refusal' when the answer is 'Sam refused to…'; 'the customer's complaint' → 'complained'. Say 'answer', 'words'.

what: Matching by topic words instead of grammar (second reader, 12 November)
reader: 'I've been to Italy twice. = I can tell you what Rome is like.' Italy → Rome. Give all left sides the same topic so only the form decides ('I used to drink coffee / I'm used to drinking coffee / …'), or do not use matching for it.

what: A one-key typo in a word copied from the task marked a correct sentence wrong (report of 12 November)
reader: 'wheh I finish the report, I'll call you.' The grader now accepts a neighbouring-key slip in a copied word (not in a last letter that can be an ending); tested in correct_part_test.php.

what: The instruction contains the answer (report of 12 November)
reader: 'Complete with will have to: Tomorrow we ___ leave early.' The learner copies the words. Give the verb in brackets and a situation (Our train is at 5 a.m., so tomorrow we ___ leave very early. (have to)).

what: An open gap with nothing that points to the answer (report of 12 November)
reader: 'Children ___ to enter without an adult.' (aren't allowed): want, need, have, are not able all fit or nearly fit. Give the situation (The sign says…) and a word bank with real forms that do not fit.

what: A word order whose cards make another correct sentence when who asks whom is not given (report of 13 November)
reader: 'she asked if I could help her': the same cards give 'I asked her if she could help'. Say who speaks to whom before the task (Anna's question to you: 'Can you help me?').

what: A long situation before an easy choice (report of 13 November)
reader: 'You want to say your report was finished in March. Choose the correct option.' Say only Choose the correct option, and put the time word in the sentence (I ___ my report last March). A situation only where the form depends on it, and then as natural as possible.

what: A typed question whose key drops words the learner may keep (report of 13 November)
reader: 'Make a question with What: You are going to cook dinner.' → What are you going to cook for dinner? is correct too. For every Make a question task, also accept the question that keeps the rest of the sentence or leaves out an extra phrase (Why did he leave?).

what: A long situation before an easy choice (report of 13 November)

task.q: You want to say your report was finished in March, and you are telling your manager about it now. Choose the correct option.
wrong: I have finished it in March.

what: A word order where an article card can move to another noun (report of 14 November)
reader: 'if you add salt the soup tastes better': the cards also give 'if you add the salt, soup tastes better', which is correct. Move every the / a card to each other noun and read the sentence; accept what is correct or change the sentence.
